$$
\prod_{M\in\mathcal R}\ell_M^{s-z}\mid A.
$$

If $n>D$, the product has weighted degree $n(s-z)>D$, contradicting $A\ne0$. Therefore $z\ge s$. A term with $Z$-degree $z$ has weighted degree at least $dz$, so $D\ge dz\ge sd$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, let $s\ge 1$ and $d\le D<p$, and let $\mathcal R$ consist of $n$ distinct affine lines. Let $A\ne0$ have weighted degree at most $D$ and satisfy $A\in I_M^s$ for every $M\in\mathcal R$. If $n>D$, then

$$
\deg_Z A\ge s
$$

and $D\ge sd$.
lemmas.title: Primitive degree cost

lemmas.proof_markdown: Write the leading $Z$-term of $A$ as $a_z(X,Y)Z^z$, where $z\ge1$ and $a_z\ne0$. Weighted degree at most $D$ gives $dz\le D<p$, and hence $1\le z<p$. Thus $z$ is nonzero in $\mathbb F_p$, so the leading term $z a_z(X,Y)Z^{z-1}$ survives formal differentiation. Therefore $A_Z\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, and let $d\le D<p$. If a polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ has weighted degree at most $D$ for weights $(1,1,d)$ and depends on $Z$, then its formal derivative satisfies

$$
A_Z=\frac{\partial A}{\partial Z}\ne0.
$$
lemmas.title: Formal derivative

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Use coordinates adapted to $M$. Because $L$ and $M$ are distinct and meet at the indicated point, $S_M(L(t))$ is a nonzero affine-linear polynomial with a simple zero at $t_0$. Moreover,

$$
W_M(L(t),P_L(t))=P_L(t)-P_M(T_M(L(t)))
$$

vanishes at $t_0$ by compatibility of the two labels. Thus both normal generators pull back to polynomials divisible by $t-t_0$. Every term belonging to $(S_M,W_M)^s$ consequently pulls back to a multiple of $(t-t_0)^s$. No derivative or factorial is divided by.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, let $s\ge1$ and $d\le D<p$, and let $M$ and $L$ be distinct affine lines with parameterizations $M(r)$ and $L(t)$. Let $P_M$ and $P_L$ have degree at most $d$. Suppose that

$$
L(t_0)=M(r_0),\qquad P_L(t_0)=P_M(r_0).
$$

If $A$ has weighted degree at most $D$ and $A\in I_M^s$, then

$$
(t-t_0)^s\mid A(L(t),P_L(t)).
$$
lemmas.title: Transverse root multiplicity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Each compatible intersection supplies the divisibility $(t-t_i)^s\mid g_L(t)$ by the transverse-root entry. The parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_h$ are distinct, so these factors are pairwise coprime and

$$
\prod_{i=1}^h(t-t_i)^s\mid g_L(t).
$$

Substituting the affine coordinates of $L(t)$ and the degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial $P_L(t)$ into a polynomial of weighted degree at most $D$ gives $\deg g_L\le D$. If $sh>D$, a nonzero $g_L$ cannot have the displayed divisor. Hence $g_L=0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, let $s\ge1$ and $d\le D<p$, and let $\mathcal R$ consist of distinct affine lines equipped with polynomials of degree at most $d$. Let $A$ have weighted degree at most $D$ and satisfy $A\in I_M^s$ for every $M\in\mathcal R$. Let $L$ be an affine line with a polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $d$. Suppose there are distinct parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_h$ and, for each $i$, a line $M_i\in\mathcal R$ with $M_i\ne L$ and a parameter $r_i$ such that

$$
L(t_i)=M_i(r_i),\qquad P_L(t_i)=P_{M_i}(r_i).
$$

If $sh>D$, then

$$
A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0.
$$
lemmas.title: Target-line transfer

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For any $D\ge d$, consider the $Z$-levels $0\le j\le\lfloor D/(2d)\rfloor$. There are more than $D/(2d)$ such levels, and each has $D-dj\ge D/2$, so it contains more than $D^2/8$ admissible monomials in $X$ and $Y$. Consequently,

$$
N_d(D)>\frac{D^3}{16d}.
$$

Also,

$$
C_s(D,d)\le\binom{s+1}{2}(D+1)\le s(s+1)D.
$$

The definition of $D_0$ gives

$$
D_0^2>16dns(s+1),
$$

and therefore $N_d(D_0)>nC_s(D_0,d)$. Homogeneous linear algebra yields a nonzero common interpolant of weighted degree at most $D_0$. Finally, $D_0<sh$ permits target-line transfer by multiplicity root counting.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, let $n\ge1$ and $s\ge1$, and let $\mathcal R$ consist of $n$ distinct affine lines equipped with polynomials of degree at most $d$. Define

$$
D_0=\left\lfloor4\sqrt{dns(s+1)}\right\rfloor+1.
$$

If $d\le D_0<p$, then there exists a nonzero polynomial $A$ of weighted degree at most $D_0$ satisfying $A\in I_M^s$ for every $M\in\mathcal R$. If, in addition, $D_0<sh$, then every target line having $h$ distinct compatible intersections with members of $\mathcal R$ satisfies

$$
A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0.
$$
lemmas.title: Explicit degree choice

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The dimension inequality supplies a nonzero common interpolant. Since $n>D$, the primitive degree entry gives $D\ge sd$. Hence every summand in $C_s(D,d)$ is active, and direct summation gives

$$
C_s(D,d)=\binom{s+1}{2}(D+1)-(d+1)\binom{s+1}{3}\ge\frac{s^2D}{6}.
$$

For $D\ge d>100$, the monomial count also satisfies

$$
N_d(D)\le\frac{2D^3}{d}.
$$

Therefore $N_d(D)>nC_s(D,d)$ implies

$$
\frac{2D^3}{d}>\frac{ns^2D}{6},
$$

and thus

$$
D^2>\frac{dns^2}{12}.
$$

The transfer condition $sh>D$ now yields

$$
h^2>\frac{D^2}{s^2}>\frac{dn}{12}.
$$

If $n=\Theta(p/\varepsilon)$ and $h=\Theta(\varepsilon p)$, substitution into this inequality gives $\varepsilon^2p^2=\Omega(dp/\varepsilon)$, equivalently $\varepsilon^3=\Omega(d/p)$. The multiplicity parameter $s$ cancels.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $100<d<p$, let $s\ge1$ and $d\le D<p$, and let $\mathcal R$ consist of $n$ distinct affine lines equipped with polynomials of degree at most $d$. Define

$$
N_d(D)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor D/d\rfloor}\binom{D-dj+2}{2},\qquad C_s(D,d)=\sum_{\substack{a,b\ge0\\a+b<s}}\max\{D-a-db+1,0\}.
$$

Suppose that

$$
n>D,\qquad N_d(D)>nC_s(D,d),\qquad sh>D.
$$

Then

$$
h^2>\frac{dn}{12}.
$$

If, along a parameter family with $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, one additionally has $n=\Theta(p/\varepsilon)$ and $h=\Theta(\varepsilon p)$, then

$$
\varepsilon^3=\Omega\!\left(\frac{d}{p}\right).
$$
lemmas.title: Rank-blind barrier

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write $C=\sum_k c_k(X,Y)Z^k$. By the definition of $e$, every positive supported exponent $k$ is divisible by $s$, and some supported $k$ has $k/s
e0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. Lucas's theorem gives $ inom{k}{r}=0$ in $\mathbb F_p$ whenever $0<r<s$, while $ inom{k}{s}=k/s
e0$ for at least one supported exponent of minimal $p$-adic valuation. Hence all lower positive Hasse derivatives vanish and $\partial_Z^{[s]}C
e0$.

The polynomial $\partial_Z^{[s]}C$ has strictly smaller $Z$-degree than the irreducible polynomial $C$, so $\gcd(C,\partial_Z^{[s]}C)=1$. Moreover, $C\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z^s]$. Since $C$ is $Z$-dependent, one of its monomials has $Z$-exponent at least $s$, and therefore $\operatorname{wdeg}C\ge ds$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Assign weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Let $C=\sum_{k\ge0}c_k(X,Y)Z^k\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be irreducible and $Z$-dependent, and define

$$e:=\min\{v_p(k):k>0,\ c_k\ne0\},\qquad s:=p^e.$$

For the Hasse derivatives determined by

$$C(X,Y,Z+T)=\sum_{r\ge0}\partial_Z^{[r]}C(X,Y,Z)T^r,$$

one has $\partial_Z^{[r]}C=0$ for every $0<r<s$, while $\partial_Z^{[s]}C\ne0$, $\gcd(C,\partial_Z^{[s]}C)=1$, and $\operatorname{wdeg}C\ge ds$.
lemmas.title: Hasse Height

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For each $i$, the definition of the height gives $C_i=E_i(X,Y,Z^{s_i})$ for some polynomial $E_i$. The graph identity implies that $W=q(t)^{s_i}$ is a root of $E_i(L(t),W)$ in $\mathbb F_p[t][W]$. Hence

$$W-q(t)^{s_i}\mid E_i(L(t),W).$$

Substituting $W=Z^{s_i}$ and using Frobenius gives

$$Z^{s_i}-q(t)^{s_i}=(Z-q(t))^{s_i}\mid C_i(L(t),Z),$$

which proves the multiplicity assertion.

The ordinary product rule gives

$$B_Z\equiv c\,C_{i,Z}\prod_{j\ne i}C_j\pmod{C_i}.$$

Because the factors are distinct and irreducible, the product over $j\ne i$ is nonzero modulo $C_i$. Thus $C_i\mid B_Z$ exactly when $C_{i,Z}=0$. By the height conclusion from [P1], this occurs exactly when $s_i>1$. Since $B$ is squarefree, its greatest common divisor with $B_Z$ therefore has precisely the asserted factors.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $B=c\prod_{i=1}^r C_i\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$, where $c\in\mathbb F_p^\times$ and the $C_i$ are distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent polynomials with Hasse heights $s_i$. If an affine-line parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $q(t)\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ satisfy

$$C_i(L(t),q(t))\equiv0,$$

then

$$(Z-q(t))^{s_i}\mid C_i(L(t),Z)$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t,Z]$. Moreover, $\gcd(B,B_Z)$ has exactly the irreducible factors $C_i$ for which $s_i>1$.
lemmas.title: Vertical Multiplicity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Assume first that both $Z$-degrees are positive. Since $U$ and $V$ are coprime, their Sylvester resultant $R(X,Y)=\operatorname{Res}_Z(U,V)$ is nonzero. Every determinant term contains $s$ coefficients of $U$ and $r$ coefficients of $V$. Weighted homogeneity therefore bounds its ordinary degree in $X,Y$ by

$$\deg R\le su+rv-drs.$$

The further inequality follows from

$$(u-dr)(v-ds)\ge0,$$

which is equivalent to $su+rv-drs\le uv/d$.

For every $L\in\mathcal T$, specialization of the Sylvester determinant gives $R(L(t))\equiv0$, because the two specialized polynomials have the common root $q_L(t)$. Thus the affine linear equation defining $L$ divides $R$. Distinct underlying lines give distinct linear factors, and a nonzero bivariate polynomial has no more distinct affine-line factors than its total degree. If one $Z$-degree is zero, the same conclusion follows directly by counting the affine-line factors of the corresponding polynomial in $X,Y$. No leading coefficient is divided out.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $U,V\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be nonzero and coprime, with

$$u=\operatorname{wdeg}U,\quad v=\operatorname{wdeg}V,\quad r=\deg_ZU,\quad s=\deg_ZV,$$

under the weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a set of distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_p^2$, each equipped with one polynomial $q_L$ of degree at most $d$, such that

$$U(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv V(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. Then

$$|\mathcal T|\le su+rv-drs\le\frac{uv}{d}.$$
lemmas.title: Weighted Resultants

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The Hasse product rule and the vanishing of all positive derivatives below order $s$ give

$$\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s=\sum_{i:s_i=s}\left(\partial_Z^{[s]}C_i\right)\prod_{\substack{j\ne i\\s_j=s}}C_j.$$

Modulo any factor $C_i$, only its displayed summand remains. That summand is nonzero modulo $C_i$ because $\gcd(C_i,\partial_Z^{[s]}C_i)=1$ and the factors are distinct. Consequently,

$$\gcd(G_s,\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s)=1.$$

The derivative has weighted degree at most $\Delta_s-ds$ and $Z$-degree at most $r_s-s$. Applying the weighted resultant bound with the latter $Z$-degree denoted by $r'$, its common-graph count is at most

$$r'\Delta_s+r_s(\Delta_s-ds)-dr_sr'.$$

Since $\Delta_s-dr_s\ge0$, this expression is maximized for $r'=r_s-s$. Substitution yields

$$(r_s-s)\Delta_s+r_s(\Delta_s-ds)-dr_s(r_s-s)=(2r_s-s)\Delta_s-dr_s^2.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $s$ be a fixed $p$-power, and let

$$G_s:=\prod_{i:s_i=s}C_i,
\qquad \Delta_s:=\operatorname{wdeg}G_s,
\qquad r_s:=\deg_ZG_s$$

for a nonempty collection of distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent factors of Hasse height $s$. For any family of affine lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels, the number of lines satisfying both formal identities

$$G_s(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0,
\qquad
\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

is at most

$$(2r_s-s)\Delta_s-dr_s^2.$$
lemmas.title: Hasse Strata

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For every graph line, the assumed identity is

$$H(L(t))B(L(t),q_L(t))=0$$

in the integral domain $\mathbb F_p[t]$. If $H(L(t))$ is nonzero, the second factor must vanish; no pointwise division by $H$ is used. A line on which $H$ vanishes identically supplies a distinct affine linear factor of the nonzero polynomial $H$, so there are at most $h$ such lines.

On every remaining line,

$$c\prod_{i=1}^r C_i(L(t),q_L(t))=0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. The integral-domain property then forces at least one factor restriction to vanish identically.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let

$$A(X,Y,Z)=H(X,Y)B(X,Y,Z),
\qquad h:=\deg H,$$

where $H\ne0$ and $B=c\prod_{i=1}^rC_i$ with $c\in\mathbb F_p^\times$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a family of affine lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels satisfying

$$A(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. At most $h$ lines in $\mathcal T$ satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$. Every other line satisfies $B(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$ and $C_i(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$ for at least one $i$.
lemmas.title: Content Removal

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If two distinct factors $C_i$ and $C_j$ vanish identically on the same graph line, the weighted resultant bound gives at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i\delta_j}{d}\right\rfloor$$

such lines. If the unique factor is $C_i$ and its selected derivative also vanishes identically, the same bound gives at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i(\delta_i-\omega_i)}{d}\right\rfloor$$

such lines, because $\operatorname{wdeg}(D_iC_i)\le\delta_i-\omega_i$ and $C_i$ is coprime to its selected nonzero derivative.

For an inseparable irreducible factor, at least one of $C_{i,X}$ and $C_{i,Y}$ is nonzero. Otherwise all three ordinary partial derivatives would vanish. Every exponent would then be divisible by $p$, and perfectness of $\mathbb F_p$ would express $C_i$ as a nontrivial $p$-th power, contradicting irreducibility.

Summing the factor-pair and factor-derivative bounds gives the first inequality by a deterministic union bound. Finally,

$$\sum_i\omega_i\delta_i=d(\Delta-\iota)+\iota$$

and

$$\sum_i\delta_i^2+\sum_{i<j}\delta_i\delta_j\le\Delta^2.$$

Substitution into the first bound, followed by integrality of $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$, gives the second bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let

$$B=c\prod_{i=1}^rC_i,
\qquad \delta_i:=\operatorname{wdeg}C_i,
\qquad \Delta:=\sum_i\delta_i,$$

where the $C_i$ are distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent factors, and let

$$\iota:=\operatorname{wdeg}\gcd(B,B_Z)=\sum_{C_{i,Z}=0}\delta_i.$$

For $C_{i,Z}\ne0$, set $D_iC_i:=C_{i,Z}$ and $\omega_i:=d$. For $C_{i,Z}=0$, at least one member of $\{C_{i,X},C_{i,Y}\}$ is nonzero; choose one as $D_iC_i$ and set $\omega_i:=1$.

Among the non-content graph lines supplied by [P5], call a line exceptional if either at least two distinct factors vanish identically on it, or exactly one factor $C_i$ vanishes identically and $D_iC_i$ also vanishes identically. The number $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$ of exceptional lines satisfies

$$N_{\mathrm{exc}}
\le
\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i(\delta_i-\omega_i)}{d}\right\rfloor
+
\sum_{i<j}\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i\delta_j}{d}\right\rfloor$$

and

$$N_{\mathrm{exc}}
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{\Delta^2-d\Delta+(d-1)\iota}{d}\right\rfloor.$$
lemmas.title: Exceptional Lines

lemmas.proof_markdown:
On a nonexceptional line of unique type $i$, each restriction

$$D_iC_i(L(t),q_L(t))
\quad\text{and}\quad
C_j(L(t),q_L(t))\ \text{for }j\ne i$$

is a nonzero polynomial in $t$. Weighted substitution bounds their respective degrees by $\delta_i-\omega_i$ and $\delta_j$. Hence the union of their root sets has size at most

$$(\delta_i-\omega_i)+\sum_{j\ne i}\delta_j=\Delta-\omega_i,$$

capped by the $p$ available parameter values.

Each removed line contributes $p$ incidences to the ambient space of $p^2(p+1)$ incidences. Multiplying each exact per-line root bound by the corresponding number of remaining lines and normalizing gives the displayed loss formula. This is a deterministic sum of root counts.

Finally, there are at most $p^2$ point vertices. Removing vertices whose current degree is at most $1$ deletes at most one incidence per such vertex, so the additional normalized loss is at most

$$\frac{p^2}{p^2(p+1)}=\frac1{p+1}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Retain the notation of [P6], and suppose at most $h$ content lines and $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$ exceptional lines have been removed. On each remaining line of unique type $i$, delete every parameter value at which $D_iC_i$ or any factor $C_j$ with $j\ne i$ vanishes. The number deleted from that line is at most

$$\min\{p,\Delta-\omega_i\}.$$

Thus a separable-type line loses at most $\min\{p,\Delta-d\}$ points, and an inseparable-type line loses at most $\min\{p,\Delta-1\}$ points. If $\sigma_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{ins}}$ are the respective numbers of remaining separable- and inseparable-type lines divided by $p(p+1)$, the deleted fraction of the ambient incidence space is at most

$$\frac{h+N_{\mathrm{exc}}}{p(p+1)}
+\sigma_{\mathrm{sep}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\Delta-d}{p}\right\}
+\sigma_{\mathrm{ins}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\Delta-1}{p}\right\}.$$

Deleting all remaining point vertices of degree at most $1$ adds at most $1/(p+1)$ to this fraction.
lemmas.title: Root Deletion

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Suppose two distinct retained graph lines meet at $(x,y,z)$. The deletion of roots of every other factor forces the two lines to have the same unique type $i$: if their types differed, the factor belonging to either line would vanish at the common point on the other line, and that point would have been deleted.

Assume that $C_{i,Z}=0$. Differentiating the two formal graph identities along their respective direction vectors $(a,b)$ gives

$$C_{i,X}(x,y,z)a+C_{i,Y}(x,y,z)b=0.$$

The two underlying affine lines are distinct and pass through the same point, so their direction vectors are independent. The two equations force

$$C_{i,X}(x,y,z)=C_{i,Y}(x,y,z)=0,$$

contradicting retention of the chosen nonzero base derivative. Hence $C_i$ is separable.

Retention also gives $C_{i,Z}(x,y,z)\ne0$ and $C_j(x,y,z)\ne0$ for every $j\ne i$. Since $C_i(x,y,z)=0$, the product rule reduces to

$$B_Z(x,y,z)=c\,C_{i,Z}(x,y,z)\prod_{j\ne i}C_j(x,y,z)\ne0.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
In the incidence system retained after [P7], let $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb F_p^3$ be incident to at least two distinct retained graph lines. Then

$$B(x,y,z)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
B_Z(x,y,z)\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Simple Intersections

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If an irreducible $Z$-dependent factor $C_i$ satisfies $C_{i,Z}=0$, every positive $Z$-exponent in $C_i$ is divisible by $p$. Such an exponent is therefore at least $p$, and the assigned weight of the corresponding $Z$-power is at least $pd$. Hence $\delta_i\ge pd$. The inequality $\Delta<pd$ excludes every such factor, so $\iota=0$ and $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.

With $\iota=0$, the content and exceptional-line bounds give at most

$$h+\frac{\Delta^2}{d}-\Delta$$

lines before taking the integer floor. Since $B$ is $Z$-dependent, $\Delta\ge d$. For fixed $a=h+\Delta$, this convex expression is maximized at $h=0$ and $\Delta=a$; the comparison of the two endpoints is

$$\frac{a^2}{d}-a-(a-d)=\frac{(a-d)^2}{d}\ge0.$$

The resulting expression $a^2/d-a$ is nondecreasing for $a\ge d$, so $a\le D$ gives the bound $\lfloor D^2/d-D\rfloor$. Every factor is separable, and the per-line deletion bound is $\Delta-d\le D-d$. The final simple-point conclusion follows from [P8].
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $B=c\prod_iC_i$ be squarefree and $Z$-dependent, with $\Delta=\operatorname{wdeg}B$ and $\iota=\operatorname{wdeg}\gcd(B,B_Z)$. If

$$\Delta<pd,$$

then

$$\iota=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gcd(B,B_Z)=1.$$

If additionally $A=HB$, $h=\deg H$, $a=h+\Delta$, and

$$a\le D<pd,$$

then the cleanup removes at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{D^2}{d}-D\right\rfloor$$

content and exceptional lines in total and at most $D-d$ parameter values from every other line. Every retained point incident to at least two retained graph lines satisfies $B_Z\ne0$.
lemmas.title: Automatic Separability

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The quoted KTZ selector and interpolation bounds are

$$n\le\frac{6400p}{\epsilon},
\qquad
D=16\bigl(\lfloor\sqrt{dn}\rfloor+1\bigr)
\le1280\left(\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}+1\right),
\qquad
D<p.$$

Since $d\ge101$, one has $D<p<pd$, so the cleanup lies automatically in the separable range of [P9]. Its normalized exceptional-line cost has scale

$$O\left(\frac{D^2}{dp^2}\right)
=O\left(\frac1{\epsilon p}+\frac1{dp^2}\right).$$

Making this cost $O(\epsilon)$ requires only $\epsilon^2p=\Omega(1)$. By contrast, both the per-line point loss and the KTZ identity-extension condition $D<k_1/2$, where $k_1=\lfloor\epsilon p/1000\rfloor$, require

$$\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}=O(\epsilon p),$$

which is equivalent to

$$\epsilon^3=\Omega\left(\frac dp\right).$$

The quoted affine-mixing loss $O(p^{-1/2})$ and the optional loss $1/(p+1)$ are weaker in the range $d\ge101$. The remaining quoted KTZ lemmas therefore apply under the same cubic premise and yield a total-degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial with global agreement at least $\epsilon/8000$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$ and degree-at-most-$d$ affine-line labels $q_L$ have local agreement

$$\epsilon:=\Pr_{L\in\mathcal L,\,x\in L}[q_L(x)=f(x)].$$

Let $C_{\mathrm{KTZ}}$ be the absolute constant in the quoted KTZ theorem. If

$$\epsilon\ge C_{\mathrm{KTZ}}\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3},$$

then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $d$ such that

$$\frac{|\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2:Q(x,y)=f(x,y)\}|}{p^2}\ge\frac{\epsilon}{8000}.$$
lemmas.title: KTZ Parameter Insertion

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Regard $F$ as a polynomial in $Z$ over $\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$. Eisenstein's criterion at the prime $X$ applies: every nonleading coefficient is divisible by $X$, while the constant coefficient $-XY^{p-1}$ is not divisible by $X^2$. Thus $F$ is irreducible in $\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ and hence squarefree. Its weighted degree is $pd$.

Formal translation gives

$$F(X,Y,Z+T)=F(X,Y,Z)+T^p,$$

so $F_Z=0$, all Hasse derivatives of orders $1$ through $p-1$ vanish, and $\partial_Z^{[p]}F=1$.

For a projective direction $[a:b]$, Frobenius in $\mathbb F_p$ gives

$$q_{a,b}(t)^p=ab^{p-1}t^p.$$

Since $X Y^{p-1}$ restricts to the same polynomial on $L_{a,b}(t)$,

$$F(L_{a,b}(t),Z)=(Z-q_{a,b}(t))^p.$$

There are $p+1$ projective directions, so their total vertical multiplicity is $p(p+1)>pd$ because $d<p$.

If a formal series $Q$ satisfied $F(X,Y,Q)=0$, then $Q^p=XY^{p-1}$. Every monomial in a Frobenius $p$-th power in $\mathbb F_p[[X,Y]]$ has both exponents divisible by $p$, whereas the exponent pair of $XY^{p-1}$ is $(1,p-1)$. This is impossible.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Define

$$F(X,Y,Z):=Z^p-XY^{p-1}.$$

Then $F$ is irreducible and squarefree, $\operatorname{wdeg}F=pd$, $F_Z=0$, $\partial_Z^{[r]}F=0$ for $1\le r<p$, and $\partial_Z^{[p]}F=1$. For every $[a:b]\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_p)$, set

$$L_{a,b}(t):=(at,bt),
\qquad
q_{a,b}(t):=ab^{p-1}t.$$

Then

$$F(L_{a,b}(t),Z)=(Z-q_{a,b}(t))^p.$$

Consequently, the multiplicity-weighted direction count is

$$p(p+1)>pd=\operatorname{wdeg}F,$$

but there is no $Q\in\mathbb F_p[[X,Y]]$ satisfying $F(X,Y,Q(X,Y))=0$.
lemmas.title: Inseparable Pencil

lemmas.proof_markdown:
On every radial line through the origin, these labels coincide with the graph labels from [P11]. Direct incidence counting is especially transparent from the rejected incidences. Every point with $y\ne0$ is accepted on all of its incident lines. Every point $(x,0)$ with $x\ne0$ is accepted on the horizontal axis and rejected on its other $p$ incident lines, while the origin is accepted everywhere. Thus there are $p(p-1)$ rejected incidences among $p^2(p+1)$ total incidences, and

$$\epsilon
=1-\frac{p(p-1)}{p^2(p+1)}
=\frac{p^2+1}{p(p+1)}.$$

The polynomial $Q=X$ has degree $1\le d$. It agrees with $f$ at all $p(p-1)$ points with $y\ne0$ and also at the origin, giving global agreement

$$\frac{p(p-1)+1}{p^2}.$$

Both agreements tend to $1$, and the exhibited global polynomial satisfies the soundness conclusion. Hence the stated counterexample claim is refuted.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Define

$$f(x,y):=xy^{p-1}.$$

Label every affine line other than the horizontal axis by the restriction of $X$, and label the horizontal axis by the constant polynomial $0$. Then this table and label family is a counterexample to affine line-versus-point soundness.
lemmas.title: Soundness Counterexample Attempt

lemmas.proof_markdown:
A uniformly selected affine line belongs to one of the chosen direction classes with probability $k/(p+1)$. On such a line the constant label $0$ agrees with $f$ at every point; on every other line the constant label $1$ disagrees at every point. Hence the local agreement is exactly

$$\epsilon=\frac{k}{p+1}.$$

The total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ at every point of $\mathbb F_p^2$. Thus the stated obstruction claim is refuted.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $0\le k\le p+1$. Set $f=0$, label every line in $k$ complete direction classes by the constant polynomial $0$, and label every other affine line by the constant polynomial $1$. Then concentration of all accepted incidences in those $k$ direction classes obstructs global recovery by a total-degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial.
lemmas.title: Direction-Concentration Attempt

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $\delta=\operatorname{wdeg}B$. Then $\deg_ZB\le\lfloor\delta/d\rfloor<p$. Suppose an irreducible polynomial $C$ divides both $B$ and $B_Z$. Writing $B=CE$, squarefreeness gives $C\nmid E$, while differentiation modulo $C$ gives $C\mid C_ZE$. Hence $C\mid C_Z$, so $C_Z=0$. In characteristic $p$, every positive $Z$-exponent of $C$ is therefore divisible by $p$. Since $\deg_ZC<p$, the polynomial $C$ is independent of $Z$, contradicting the primitivity of $B$. Thus $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.

The strict threshold is sharp: $Z^p-X$ is primitive, squarefree, smooth, and absolutely irreducible, has weighted degree $dp$, and has zero $Z$-derivative.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$. If $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ is squarefree, primitive as a polynomial in $Z$, and satisfies $\operatorname{wdeg}B<dp$, then $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.
lemmas.title: Vertical separability

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write $U=\sum_iU_iZ^i$ and $V=\sum_jV_jZ^j$. The weighted-degree constraints give $\deg U_i\le u-di$ and $\deg V_j\le v-dj$. The nonzero resultant $R=\operatorname{Res}_Z(U,V)$ is homogeneous of degree $s$ in the coefficients of $U$ and degree $r$ in those of $V$. Every resultant monomial has total vertical-index weight $rs$, so its ordinary $(X,Y)$-degree is at most $su+rv-drs$. Hence $\deg R\le su+rv-drs$.

For each $L\in\mathcal T$, the specialized polynomials $U(L(t),Z)$ and $V(L(t),Z)$ have the common factor $Z-P_L(t)$, so $R(L(t))\equiv0$. The affine linear equation of $L$ therefore divides $R$. Distinct lines give distinct factors, proving the bound. No leading coefficient is divided out.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Let $U,V\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be nonzero and coprime, with $u=\operatorname{wdeg}U$, $v=\operatorname{wdeg}V$, $r=\deg_ZU$, and $s=\deg_ZV$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a family of distinct affine lines with parametrizations $L(t)$ and labels $P_L\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ of degree at most $d$ such that $U(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv V(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every $L\in\mathcal T$. Then $|\mathcal T|\le su+rv-drs$.
lemmas.title: Weighted resultant bound

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Frobenius acts transitively on the $k$ absolute factors of $C$. It preserves weighted and vertical degrees, so every factor has weighted degree $\delta/k$ and vertical degree $r/k$. Since the product of their graph restrictions vanishes in the domain $\overline{\mathbb F}_p[t]$, at least one factor vanishes on each graph. Applying Frobenius to that identity shows that every conjugate vanishes there.

Two distinct conjugates are coprime. Applying [P2] after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ gives $|\mathcal T|\le 2(r/k)(\delta/k)-d(r/k)^2=(2r\delta-dr^2)/k^2$. Finally, $\delta^2/d-(2r\delta-dr^2)=(\delta-dr)^2/d\ge0$. Since $k\ge2$, the last two bounds follow.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with weights $(1,1,d)$. Let $C\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be irreducible and $Z$-dependent, with $\delta=\operatorname{wdeg}C$, $r=\deg_ZC$, and exactly $k\ge2$ absolute factors. If $\mathcal T$ is a family of distinct affine $\mathbb F_p$-lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels $P_L$ satisfying $C(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, then $|\mathcal T|\le(2r\delta-dr^2)/k^2\le\delta^2/(dk^2)\le\delta^2/(4d)$.
lemmas.title: Frobenius purification

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Primitivity excludes base-only irreducible factors. Assign each line in $\mathcal T$ to one geometrically reducible factor supporting it. If the distinct assigned factors have weighted degrees $\delta_i$, then [P3] gives at most $\delta_i^2/(4d)$ assigned lines for the $i$th factor. Therefore $|\mathcal T|\le\sum_i\delta_i^2/(4d)\le(\sum_i\delta_i)^2/(4d)\le D^2/(4d)$. This is the sole union loss.

For sharpness, $C$ has vertical degree $2$ and weighted degree $2d$. It is irreducible over $\mathbb F_p$: a factorization would make $
u H_0^2$ a square in $\mathbb F_p(X,Y)$ and hence make $
u$ a square. Over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$, it splits into $Z-\sqrt
u H_0$ and $Z+\sqrt
u H_0$. Each of the $d$ base lines dividing $H_0$, with label zero, is a graph line. On any other line, a graph label $q_L$ would give $(q_L/H_0(L))^2=
u$ in $\mathbb F_p(t)$, which is impossible. Thus exactly $d$ graph lines occur.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with weights $(1,1,d)$. Let $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be primitive in $Z$ and satisfy $\operatorname{wdeg}B\le D$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a family of distinct affine $\mathbb F_p$-lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels such that every $L\in\mathcal T$ is supported by an $\mathbb F_p$-irreducible, geometrically reducible factor of $B$. Then $|\mathcal T|\le D^2/(4d)$. If additionally $p>2d$, $\nu\in\mathbb F_p^\times$ is a nonsquare, and $H_0$ is a product of $d$ distinct affine-line equations, then $C=Z^2-\nu H_0^2$ is $\mathbb F_p$-irreducible with two absolute factors and supports exactly $d=(2d)^2/(4d)$ degree-at-most-$d$ graph lines.
lemmas.title: Factor aggregation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Fix $(L,\tau)\in\mathcal E$, write $w=(L(\tau),f(L(\tau)))$, and let $v_L=(v_{L,1},v_{L,2})$ be the direction of $L$. Differentiating the formal graph identity gives $B_X(w)v_{L,1}+B_Y(w)v_{L,2}+B_Z(w)P_L'(\tau)=0$. Ramification gives $B_Z(w)=0$, while smoothness gives $(B_X(w),B_Y(w))\ne(0,0)$. Thus $v_L$ lies in the unique projective kernel direction of the nonzero functional $(B_X(w),B_Y(w))$.

All accepted incidences above a fixed base point have the same lift $(x,f(x))$. Hence that point permits at most one affine graph line. Summing over the $p^2$ base points gives $|\mathcal E|\le p^2$. Division by the ambient $p^2(p+1)$ incidences gives the normalized bound. No derivative is divided by.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Let $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$, let $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$, and let $\mathcal T$ be a family of affine lines parametrized by $L(t)$ with labels $P_L\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ of degree at most $d$ satisfying $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. Let $\mathcal E$ be the set of pairs $(L,\tau)$ satisfying $P_L(\tau)=f(L(\tau))$ and $B_Z(L(\tau),P_L(\tau))=0$. If every lift $(L(\tau),P_L(\tau))$ belonging to $\mathcal E$ is smooth on $B=0$, then $|\mathcal E|\le p^2$, and $|\mathcal E|/[p^2(p+1)]\le1/(p+1)$.
lemmas.title: Smooth ramification sparsity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Since $D<2d$ and $B$ is $Z$-dependent, $B=a(X,Y)Z+b(X,Y)$ with $\deg a\le D-d$ and $\deg b\le D$. Primitivity gives $\gcd(a,b)=1$, and Gauss's lemma makes this primitive linear polynomial absolutely irreducible.

Because $B_Z=a$, a base point admits a ramified lift exactly when $a=b=0$. Bézout's theorem therefore bounds the ramified base set by $\deg a\deg b\le D(D-d)$. Deleting all these base vertices removes normalized incidence mass at most $D(D-d)/p^2$.

If a graph line were identically ramified, then $a(L(t))\equiv0$; substituting into $B(L(t),P(t))\equiv0$ gives $b(L(t))\equiv0$. The line equation would divide both $a$ and $b$, contradicting their coprimality.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $d\le D<2d$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$. Let $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be primitive in $Z$, $Z$-dependent, and satisfy $\operatorname{wdeg}B\le D$. Then $|\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2:\exists z\in\mathbb F_p,\ B(x,y,z)=B_Z(x,y,z)=0\}|\le D(D-d)$, and there is no affine-line parametrization $L(t)$ with a degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial $P(t)$ satisfying both $B(L(t),P(t))\equiv0$ and $B_Z(L(t),P(t))\equiv0$.
lemmas.title: Linear vertical regime

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The definitions give $\deg H=2s+e=d+1=D$, so $\operatorname{wdeg}B=D<p$. The coefficients $X$ and $H(Y)$ are coprime. Thus $B$ is primitive in $Z$, and Gauss's lemma, equivalently the linear regime of [P6], makes $B$ absolutely irreducible. Hence it is squarefree.

Direct differentiation gives $B_Z=X$, and $\gcd(B,X)=1$ because $X\nmid H(Y)$. This also follows from [P1] since $D<dp$. For a degree-one polynomial, the normalized discriminant is $1$, whereas $\operatorname{Res}_Z(B,B_Z)=X$. Its zero set is the affine line $X=0$, which is smooth and absolutely irreducible.

For every $j$, one has $B(0,c_j,0)=0$ and $B_X(0,c_j,0)=0$, $B_Y(0,c_j,0)=H'(c_j)=0$, and $B_Z(0,c_j,0)=0$. The equality $H'(c_j)=0$ follows from the double factor $(Y-c_j)^2$, so every displayed lift is singular.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d\le p-2$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$, and set $D=d+1$, $s=\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$, and $e=d+1-2s\in\{0,1\}$. Choose distinct $c_1,\ldots,c_s\in\mathbb F_p$. If $e=1$, choose $b\in\mathbb F_p\setminus\{c_1,\ldots,c_s\}$, and define $H(Y)=\prod_{j=1}^s(Y-c_j)^2(Y-b)^e$ and $B(X,Y,Z)=XZ+H(Y)$, with the last factor omitted when $e=0$. Then $B$ is primitive in $Z$, squarefree, and absolutely irreducible, with $\operatorname{wdeg}B=D<p$, $B_Z=X$, and $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$. Its normalized degree-one discriminant is $1$, while $\operatorname{Res}_Z(B,B_Z)=X$, whose zero set is a smooth absolutely irreducible affine line. For every $1\le j\le s$, the point $(0,c_j,0)$ is singular on $B=0$.
lemmas.title: Singular construction algebra

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For $m\ne0$, the factor $(Y-c_j)^2$ shows that $H(c_j+mt)$ is divisible by $t^2$; for $m=0$, it is identically zero. Hence each displayed quotient is a polynomial of degree at most $d$ and vanishes at $t=0$. Substitution gives $B(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))=t(-H(c_j+mt)/t)+H(c_j+mt)\equiv0$.

If $t\ne0$, the definition of $f$ gives $P_{j,m}(t)=f(t,c_j+mt)$. At $t=0$, both sides equal $0$. Thus every selected line is fully accepted. The selected base lines have equations $Y=c_j+mX$, so distinct pairs $(j,m)$ give distinct lines. Their number is $sp>D$, and their $sp^2$ accepted incidences have normalized mass $sp^2/[p^2(p+1)]=s/(p+1)$.

Finally, $B_Z(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))=t$, so exactly $t=0$ is ramified on each selected line. The $sp$ selected ramified incidences have normalized mass $sp/[p^2(p+1)]=s/[p(p+1)]$. The quotient defining $P_{j,m}$ is exact polynomial division; no value at $t=0$ is obtained by inversion.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Under the hypotheses and notation of [P7], for $1\le j\le s$ and $m\in\mathbb F_p$ define $L_{j,m}(t)=(t,c_j+mt)$ and $P_{j,m}(t)=-H(c_j+mt)/t$. Define $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$ by $f(x,y)=-H(y)/x$ when $x\ne0$ and $f(0,y)=0$, and give every unselected affine line the constant label $0$. Then every $P_{j,m}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $d$ satisfying $B(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))\equiv0$, and every one of the $sp>D$ selected lines is fully accepted by $f$. Their uniform line measure is $s/(p+1)$, so the table's agreement is at least $s/(p+1)$. Moreover, $B_Z(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))=t$, so each selected line has exactly one ramified accepted parameter, and the normalized mass of the selected ramified incidences is $s/[p(p+1)]$.
lemmas.title: Explicit incidence table

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Suppose such a polynomial $Q$ existed. Then $R(X,Y)=XQ(X,Y)+H(Y)$ would have total degree at most $D=d+1$. For every selected line, $R(L_{j,m}(t))=B(L_{j,m}(t),Q(L_{j,m}(t)))=B(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))\equiv0$. Thus the defining linear polynomial of each of the $sp>D$ distinct selected lines would divide $R$. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $D$ cannot have more than $D$ distinct affine-line factors, so $R=0$. This would imply $X\mid H(Y)$, a contradiction.

Now let $A$ be a graph interpolant of weighted degree at most $d$. Since $Z$ has weight $d$, it has the form $A(X,Y,Z)=aZ+b(X,Y)$, where $a\in\mathbb F_p$ and $\deg b\le d$. If $a=0$, then $b$ vanishes identically on more than $d$ distinct lines and hence $b=0$. If $a\ne0$, the polynomial $Q=-a^{-1}b$ has total degree at most $d$ and restricts to every selected label, contradicting the first part. Hence no nonzero interpolant has weighted degree at most $d$. Entry [P7] supplies the interpolant $B$ of weighted degree $D=d+1$, proving minimality.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Under the hypotheses and notation of [P8], there is no polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $d$ such that $Q(L_{j,m}(t))\equiv P_{j,m}(t)$ for every $1\le j\le s$ and $m\in\mathbb F_p$. Moreover, every nonzero $A\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ satisfying $A(L_{j,m}(t),P_{j,m}(t))\equiv0$ for all selected lines has weighted degree at least $D=d+1$. Consequently, $B=XZ+H(Y)$ is a minimum-weight graph interpolant for the selected graph lines.
lemmas.title: Interpolation minimality

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The polynomial $A$ has degree $r=D-d$. Hence $\operatorname{wdeg}(Z^2)=2d$ and $\operatorname{wdeg}(AZ)=r+d=D$; since $2d\le D$, one has $\operatorname{wdeg}B_{\mathrm{sm}}=D$. As a degree-one polynomial in $Y$, $B_{\mathrm{sm}}$ is absolutely irreducible, and $(B_{\mathrm{sm}})_Y=1$ makes its hypersurface smooth. Since $p$ is odd, $(\Delta_{\mathrm{sm}})_Y=-4\ne0$. The discriminant is also degree one in $Y$, so it is smooth and absolutely irreducible.

On the displayed graph, $B_{\mathrm{sm}}(t,0,0)=0$, while $(B_{\mathrm{sm}})_Z(t,0,0)=A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(t-a_i)$. The $a_i$ are distinct, so this restriction has exactly $r=D-d$ roots. All corresponding lifts are smooth because $(B_{\mathrm{sm}})_Y=1$. This is consistent with [P5]: the roots occur at distinct base points, with only one displayed graph direction through each.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $2d\le D<p$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$, set $r=D-d$, choose distinct $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in\mathbb F_p$, and define $A(X)=\prod_{i=1}^r(X-a_i)$ and $B_{\mathrm{sm}}(X,Y,Z)=Z^2+A(X)Z+Y$. Then $B_{\mathrm{sm}}$ is monic in $Z$, has weighted degree $D$, and is smooth and absolutely irreducible. Its $Z$-discriminant $\Delta_{\mathrm{sm}}(X,Y)=A(X)^2-4Y$ is also smooth and absolutely irreducible. The label $P_L(t)=0$ on the line $L(t)=(t,0)$ satisfies $B_{\mathrm{sm}}(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, and $(B_{\mathrm{sm}})_Z(L(t),P_L(t))=A(t)$ has exactly $D-d$ distinct roots.
lemmas.title: Monic stress test

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Both terms of $B_{\mathrm{den}}$ have weighted degree $2d=D$. Over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p(X,Y)$, the element $XYg(X)^2$ is not a square because its valuation at $Y$ is odd. Since $p$ is odd, $Z^2-XYg(X)^2$ is irreducible over that field. Gauss's lemma makes $B_{\mathrm{den}}$ absolutely irreducible. It is squarefree and primitive, and [P1] applies because $D=2d<dp$.

For each nonzero square $s=c_s^2$, one has $P_s(t)^2=c_s^2t^2g(t)^2=st^2g(t)^2$, which equals $XYg(X)^2$ after substituting $(X,Y)=(t,st)$. Thus the graph identity holds, and the label has degree $d$. There are $(p-1)/2$ nonzero squares, while $(p-1)/2>2d=D$.

Since $(B_{\mathrm{den}})_Z=2Z$, its restriction to a graph is $2c_stg(t)$, whose distinct roots are $0,a_1,\ldots,a_{d-1}$. At each corresponding lift, $Z=0$, and either $X=Y=0$ or $g(X)=0$. The derivatives $(B_{\mathrm{den}})_X=-Yg^2-2XYgg'$, $(B_{\mathrm{den}})_Y=-Xg^2$, and $(B_{\mathrm{den}})_Z=2Z$ therefore all vanish, so every ramified lift is singular.

Finally, a polynomial root would satisfy $Q(X,Y)^2=XYg(X)^2$. The valuation at $Y$ is even on the left and equal to $1$ on the right, which is impossible.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $d\ge101$, and assume $p>4d+1$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$, set $D=2d$, choose distinct nonzero $a_1,\ldots,a_{d-1}\in\mathbb F_p$, and define $g(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}(X-a_i)$ and $B_{\mathrm{den}}(X,Y,Z)=Z^2-XYg(X)^2$. Then $B_{\mathrm{den}}$ has weighted degree $D$ and is absolutely irreducible. For every nonzero square $s\in\mathbb F_p$, choose $c_s\in\mathbb F_p^\times$ with $c_s^2=s$ and set $L_s(t)=(t,st)$ and $P_s(t)=c_stg(t)$. Each $P_s$ has degree $d$ and satisfies $B_{\mathrm{den}}(L_s(t),P_s(t))\equiv0$. There are $(p-1)/2>D$ such graph lines. On every one, $(B_{\mathrm{den}})_Z$ vanishes at exactly the $d=D-d$ parameters $0,a_1,\ldots,a_{d-1}$, and every corresponding lift is singular on $B_{\mathrm{den}}=0$. There is no $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ satisfying $B_{\mathrm{den}}(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0$.
lemmas.title: Dense singular pencil

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Entries [P7]–[P9] give an absolutely irreducible interpolant of weight $D$ supporting $sp>D$ graph lines, but [P9] rules out a total-degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial restricting to all their labels; the equation $XQ+H=0$ also rules out a polynomial root. Entry [P11] supplies another absolutely irreducible example with more than $D$ graph directions and no polynomial root. These examples refute the first assertion.

For [P7] and [P8], $\operatorname{Res}_Z(B,B_Z)=X$ is a smooth absolutely irreducible line. Nevertheless, for each $j$, all $p$ lines indexed by $m\in\mathbb F_p$ pass through the same ramified lift $(0,c_j,0)$. This refutes the second assertion.

In [P10], the interpolant is monic and both its hypersurface and its discriminant are smooth and absolutely irreducible, while the displayed graph line contains exactly $D-d$ ramified parameters. This is not $o(D-d)$ and refutes the third assertion.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and give $X,Y,Z$ weights $(1,1,d)$. The following assertions hold:

1. If an absolutely irreducible graph interpolant of weighted degree at most $D<p$ supports more than $D$ distinct affine graph lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels, then it has a polynomial root $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $d$ satisfying $B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0$, without any simple-common-lift hypothesis.

2. Smooth absolute irreducibility of the raw-resultant curve $\operatorname{Res}_Z(B,B_Z)=0$ controls the number of graph directions meeting a ramified lifted point.

3. If $2d\le D<p$, a graph interpolant is monic in $Z$, and its $Z$-discriminant is smooth and absolutely irreducible, then every degree-at-most-$d$ graph line contains $o(D-d)$ parameters at which $B_Z$ vanishes.
lemmas.title: Simplicity substitutes

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Applying [P3] to the geometrically reducible factors of weights $\delta_i$ and summing gives at most $\sum_i\delta_i^2/(4d)\le D^2/(4d)$ removed graph lines. After uniform-incidence normalization, their cost is at most $D^2/[4dp(p+1)]=O(1/(\epsilon p))$ under the stated envelope. Entry [P5] bounds the smooth ramified incidences for a fixed assigned factor by $p^2$, hence by normalized mass $1/(p+1)$. These estimates require the stated factor assignment and lifted-point smoothness; [P12] shows that absolute irreducibility alone does not supply the latter.

If the remaining singular incidences are deleted using the per-line budget, their normalized cost is $O(D/p)=O(\sqrt{d/(\epsilon p)})$. Requiring this quantity to be $O(\epsilon)$ gives $\sqrt{d/(\epsilon p)}=O(\epsilon)$, which is equivalent, up to absolute constants, to $\epsilon^3=\Omega(d/p)$. The calculation is conditional on this deletion architecture and does not give a lower bound for methods that globally control singular accepted lifts.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $0<\epsilon\le1$. Suppose the interpolation weight satisfies $D=O(\sqrt{dp/\epsilon})$. Suppose a deletion argument assigns supported graph lines to fixed $\mathbb F_p$-irreducible factors, deletes graph lines supported on geometrically reducible factors using [P3], applies [P5] only to ramified lifts known to be smooth on their assigned factor, and charges every remaining singular ramified incidence by the per-line budget $D/p$. Then the normalized purification loss is $O(1/(\epsilon p))$, the normalized smooth-ramification loss for each fixed assigned factor is at most $1/(p+1)$, and the singular-ramification loss is $O(D/p)=O(\sqrt{d/(\epsilon p)})$. Requiring the last loss to be $O(\epsilon)$ imposes $\epsilon^3=\Omega(d/p)$.
lemmas.title: Singular deletion scale

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If some $C_i$ were independent of $Z$, then $C_i\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ would divide every coefficient of $B$ viewed as a polynomial in $Z$, contradicting primitivity. Hence $r_i>0$.

The weighted-degree bound gives

$$
d r_i\le \delta_i\le \delta<p,
$$

so $1\le r_i<p$. The derivative of the leading $Z$-term is therefore nonzero, and

$$
C_{i,Z}\ne0,
\qquad
\deg_Z(C_{i,Z})=r_i-1<r_i.
$$

Since $C_i$ is irreducible, any nonconstant common divisor of $C_i$ and $C_{i,Z}$ would be associated to $C_i$, which is impossible because $C_{i,Z}$ has smaller $Z$-degree. Thus $\gcd(C_i,C_{i,Z})=1$. Absolute irreducibility is not used.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $1,1,d$, respectively. Let $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be primitive in $Z$, squarefree, of positive $Z$-degree and weighted degree $\delta<p$, and write

$$
B=c\prod_{i=1}^{s}C_i,
\qquad c\in\mathbb F_p^\times,
$$

where the $C_i$ are distinct irreducible polynomials. For

$$
\delta_i=\operatorname{wdeg}(C_i),
\qquad
r_i=\deg_Z(C_i),
$$

every $i\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$ satisfies

$$
r_i\ge1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gcd(C_i,C_{i,Z})=1.
$$
lemmas.title: Factor separability

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Weighted degree gives

$$
\deg_{X,Y}(u_a)\le u-da,
\qquad
\deg_{X,Y}(v_b)\le v-db
$$

for every nonzero coefficient. Every monomial in the Sylvester determinant contains $s$ coefficients of $U$ and $r$ coefficients of $V$, and the aggregate coefficient-index sum is $rs$. Its base degree is consequently at most

$$
su+rv-drs.
$$

Taking the sum of the determinant monomials cannot increase this bound. This calculation uses the Sylvester determinant directly and divides by no leading coefficient. If one $Z$-degree is $0$, the formula is the direct degree bound for the corresponding base polynomial. Because the determinant is polynomial in the coefficients, the calculation remains valid under specialization even when a leading coefficient vanishes or the specialized $Z$-degree drops.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $1,1,d$, respectively. Let

$$
U=\sum_{a=0}^{r}u_a(X,Y)Z^a,
\qquad
V=\sum_{b=0}^{s}v_b(X,Y)Z^b
$$

be nonzero polynomials in $\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ satisfying

$$
\deg_Z(U)=r,
\qquad
\deg_Z(V)=s,
\qquad
\operatorname{wdeg}(U)=u,
\qquad
\operatorname{wdeg}(V)=v.
$$

With the convention $\deg_{X,Y}(0)=-\infty$,

$$
\deg_{X,Y}\operatorname{Res}_Z(U,V)\le su+rv-drs.
$$
lemmas.title: Weighted resultant degree

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Factor separability gives $\gcd(C_i,C_{i,Z})=1$, so the $Z$-resultant $R_i$ is nonzero. Moreover,

$$
\deg_Z(C_i)=r_i,
\qquad
\deg_Z(C_{i,Z})=r_i-1.
$$

The weighted resultant bound applied to $C_i$ and $C_{i,Z}$ gives

$$
\deg_{X,Y}(R_i)
\le (r_i-1)\delta_i+r_i\gamma_i-dr_i(r_i-1)
=\Xi_i.
$$

For every $L\in\mathcal E_i$, both pullbacks vanish identically. Specializing the Sylvester determinant to the base line therefore gives

$$
R_i(x_L(t),y_L(t))\equiv0,
$$

including when the specialized $Z$-degree drops. Hence $\ell_L$ divides $R_i$ and $\nu_L\ge1$. The base lines are distinct, so their affine-linear factors are pairwise nonassociate. Consequently,

$$
\sum_{L\in\mathcal E_i}\nu_L
\le \deg_{X,Y}(R_i)
\le\Xi_i.
$$

The cardinality bound follows from $\nu_L\ge1$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Assume the hypotheses and notation of researcher-0007:P1.1. Fix $i$ and put

$$
\gamma_i=\operatorname{wdeg}(C_{i,Z}),
\qquad
R_i=\operatorname{Res}_Z(C_i,C_{i,Z}),
$$

and

$$
\Xi_i=(r_i-1)\delta_i+r_i\gamma_i-dr_i(r_i-1).
$$

Let $\mathcal T_i$ be a family indexed by distinct affine lines with equations $\ell_L(X,Y)=0$. For each $L\in\mathcal T_i$, let $L(t)=(x_L(t),y_L(t))$ be an affine-linear parametrization and let $P_L\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ satisfy $\deg P_L\le d$ and

$$
C_i(x_L(t),y_L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0.
$$

Define

$$
\mathcal E_i=
\left\{L\in\mathcal T_i:
C_{i,Z}(x_L(t),y_L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0
\right\}
$$

and, for $L\in\mathcal E_i$,

$$
\nu_L=\operatorname{ord}_{\ell_L}(R_i).
$$

Then

$$
R_i\ne0,
\qquad
\deg_{X,Y}(R_i)\le\Xi_i,
\qquad
\sum_{L\in\mathcal E_i}\nu_L\le\Xi_i.
$$

In particular,

$$
|\mathcal E_i|\le\min\{|\mathcal T_i|,\Xi_i\}.
$$
lemmas.title: Exceptional graph lines

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every monomial of $C_{i,Z}$ has weighted degree at most $\gamma_i$. Under the substitutions

$$
X=x_L(t),
\qquad
Y=y_L(t),
\qquad
Z=P_L(t),
$$

the degrees of the $X$- and $Y$-factors are at most their exponents, while the degree contributed by a $Z$-factor is at most $d$ times its exponent. Hence

$$
\deg G_{i,L}\le\gamma_i.
$$

The sum of the orders of any collection of roots of a nonzero univariate polynomial is at most its degree, proving the stated inequality. For any point table $f$, accepted incidences at which $C_{i,Z}(L(t),f(L(t)))=0$ are a subset of these roots because acceptance gives $P_L(t)=f(L(t))$. Thus the orders provide the full local polar-intersection charge. No factorial, ordinary higher derivative, or Hasse-derivative denominator is used.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let the objects satisfy the hypotheses of researcher-0007:P3.1. For $L\in\mathcal T_i\setminus\mathcal E_i$, set

$$
G_{i,L}(t)=C_{i,Z}(x_L(t),y_L(t),P_L(t)).
$$

Then $G_{i,L}\ne0$ and

$$
\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_p}
\operatorname{ord}_{t=\alpha}G_{i,L}(t)
\le\gamma_i.
$$
lemmas.title: Finite polar intersections

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The exceptional graph-line bound gives

$$
e_i\le\min\{|\mathcal T_i|,\Xi_i\}.
$$

An exceptional line has $p$ parameter values and therefore contributes at most $p$ accepted incidences. On a nonexceptional line, acceptance identifies $f(L(t))$ with $P_L(t)$, so the finite polar-intersection bound limits the ramified accepted incidences, with multiplicity, by $\gamma_i$. Thus

$$
|\mathcal R|
\le
\sum_i\left(pe_i+(|\mathcal T_i|-e_i)\gamma_i\right).
$$

Bounding $e_i$ by $\min\{|\mathcal T_i|,\Xi_i\}$, discarding the nonpositive terms $-e_i\gamma_i$, and dividing by $p^2(p+1)$ gives the normalized bound.

Formal differentiation with respect to $Z$ lowers weighted degree by at least $d$, so

$$
\gamma_i\le\delta_i-d.
$$

Substitution into $\Xi_i$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Xi_i
&\le(r_i-1)\delta_i+r_i(\delta_i-d)-dr_i(r_i-1)\\
&=(2r_i-1)\delta_i-dr_i^2\\
&=\frac{\delta_i^2}{d}-\delta_i-
\frac{(\delta_i-dr_i)^2}{d}\\
&\le\frac{\delta_i^2}{d}-\delta_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Weighted degree is additive under products, so

$$
\sum_i\delta_i=\delta,
\qquad
\sum_i\delta_i^2\le\delta^2.
$$

It follows that

$$
\sum_i\Xi_i\le\frac{\delta^2}{d}-\delta.
$$

Finally,

$$
\sum_i\frac{|\mathcal T_i|\gamma_i}{p^2(p+1)}
=\frac1p\sum_i\tau_i\gamma_i
\le\frac1p\sum_i\tau_i(\delta_i-d)
=\frac{\tau(\bar\delta-d)}p.
$$

Combining these estimates yields the coarse bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Give $X,Y,Z$ weights $1,1,d$, respectively. Let $B\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be primitive in $Z$, squarefree, of positive $Z$-degree and weighted degree $\delta<p$, with

$$
B=c\prod_{i=1}^{s}C_i.
$$

For each $i$, put

$$
\delta_i=\operatorname{wdeg}(C_i),
\quad
r_i=\deg_Z(C_i),
\quad
\gamma_i=\operatorname{wdeg}(C_{i,Z}),
$$

and

$$
\Xi_i=(r_i-1)\delta_i+r_i\gamma_i-dr_i(r_i-1).
$$

Let $\mathcal T=\bigsqcup_i\mathcal T_i$ be a disjoint assignment of distinct affine lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels $P_L$, satisfying

$$
C_i(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0
\qquad(L\in\mathcal T_i).
$$

For each $i$, let

$$
e_i=
\left|
\left\{L\in\mathcal T_i:
C_{i,Z}(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0
\right\}
\right|.
$$

For a point table $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$, let $i(L)=i$ when $L\in\mathcal T_i$, and define

$$
\mathcal R=
\left\{(L,t):
\begin{array}{l}
L\in\mathcal T,\ t\in\mathbb F_p,\\
P_L(t)=f(L(t)),\\
C_{i(L),Z}(L(t),f(L(t)))=0
\end{array}
\right\}.
$$

Then

$$
e_i\le\min\{|\mathcal T_i|,\Xi_i\},
$$

$$
|\mathcal R|
\le
\sum_i\left(pe_i+(|\mathcal T_i|-e_i)\gamma_i\right),
$$

and

$$
\frac{|\mathcal R|}{p^2(p+1)}
\le
\sum_i\frac{\min\{|\mathcal T_i|,\Xi_i\}}{p(p+1)}
+
\sum_i\frac{|\mathcal T_i|\gamma_i}{p^2(p+1)}.
$$

Moreover,

$$
\gamma_i\le\delta_i-d
$$

and

$$
\Xi_i\le(2r_i-1)\delta_i-dr_i^2
\le\frac{\delta_i^2}{d}-\delta_i.
$$

If

$$
\tau_i=\frac{|\mathcal T_i|}{p(p+1)},
\qquad
\tau=\sum_i\tau_i>0,
\qquad
\bar\delta=\frac{\sum_i\tau_i\delta_i}{\tau},
$$

then

$$
\frac{|\mathcal R|}{p^2(p+1)}
\le
\frac{\delta^2/d-\delta}{p(p+1)}
+
\frac{\tau(\bar\delta-d)}p.
$$
lemmas.title: Factorwise cleanup bounds

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For every edge $(x,L)\in E'$, the assigned graph identity and acceptance imply

$$
C_i(x,f(x))=0.
$$

The cleaned-edge hypothesis gives $C_{i,Z}(x,f(x))\ne0$, so this is a simple $Z$-root. Choose $b\in\mathcal X$. At least $k>\delta_i$ graph lines of the component pass through $b$. The simple-root Newton recursion from KTZ Lemmas 2.7 and 6.1, applied with weighted degree $\delta_i$, constructs a polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $d$, agrees with every incident line label, and satisfies

$$
C_i(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0.
$$

The recursion divides only by the certified nonzero scalar $C_{i,Z}(b,f(b))$. Simple-root uniqueness propagates the same $Q$ throughout the connected component, yielding $Q(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$.

For the density bound, put

$$
a=\frac{|\mathcal X|}{p^2},
\qquad
b_0=\frac{|T'|}{p(p+1)},
\qquad
\rho=\frac{|E'|}{p^2(p+1)},
$$

and

$$
\kappa=\frac{k}{p},
\qquad
u=\frac1{\sqrt{p+1}}.
$$

Minimum degree and affine incidence mixing give

$$
\rho\ge\frac{\kappa a}{2},
\qquad
\rho\ge\kappa b_0,
\qquad
\rho\le ab_0+\nu\sqrt{ab_0}.
$$

The mixing hypothesis is $\nu\le\kappa/4$. If $a<\kappa/4$, the second and third inequalities imply $b_0<a/9$; substituting this into the upper bound contradicts $\rho\ge\kappa a/2$. If $b_0<\kappa/4$, the first and third inequalities imply $a<b_0$; substitution contradicts $\rho\ge\kappa b_0$. Therefore

$$
a,b_0\ge\frac\kappa4.
$$

Since $Q=f$ on $\mathcal X$, its global agreement is at least $a\ge k/(4p)$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Assume the hypotheses and notation of researcher-0007:P5.1, and fix $i$. Let $G=(\mathcal X,T',E')$ be a connected bipartite graph with $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb F_p^2$, $T'\subseteq\mathcal T_i$, and

$$
E'\subseteq
\{(x,L)\in\mathcal X\times T':x\in L,\ P_L(x)=f(x)\}.
$$

Suppose $G$ has minimum degree at least the integer $k$, and suppose

$$
C_{i,Z}(x,f(x))\ne0
\qquad((x,L)\in E').
$$

If

$$
k>\delta_i
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac1{\sqrt{p+1}}\le\frac{k}{4p},
$$

then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $d$ such that

$$
Q(x)=f(x)
\qquad(x\in\mathcal X)
$$

and

$$
\frac{|\{x\in\mathbb F_p^2:Q(x)=f(x)\}|}{p^2}
\ge\frac{k}{4p}.
$$
lemmas.title: Cleaned factor component

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Since $D\ge2d$, one has $e\ge d$. Expanding $B$ gives

$$
B=Z^2-ZH(X),
$$

and hence

$$
\operatorname{wdeg}(B)
=\max\{2d,d+e\}=D.
$$

The distinct factors $Z$ and $Z-H(X)$ make $B$ squarefree, and the coefficient of $Z^2$ is $1$, so $B$ is primitive in $Z$.

Because $p>d\ge101$, the value $2$ differs from both $0$ and $1$ in $\mathbb F_p$. Thus no vertical line has an accepted point. On a nonvertical line, the $X$-coordinate has the form

$$
x_L(t)=u+vt,
\qquad v\ne0,
$$

so it runs bijectively through $\mathbb F_p$. The line therefore contains exactly $|S|=e$ parameters for which $f(L(t))=0=P_L(t)$. Moreover,

$$
B(L(t),P_L(t))=B(L(t),0)\equiv0.
$$

There are $p^2$ nonvertical affine lines. The accepted-incidence count is consequently $ep^2$, while the full incidence count is $p^2(p+1)$. Division gives $\varepsilon=e/(p+1)=(D-d)/(p+1)$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, and let $d,D$ be integers satisfying

$$
101\le d,
\qquad
2d\le D<p.
$$

Put $e=D-d$, choose $S\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ with $|S|=e$, and define

$$
H(X)=\prod_{a\in S}(X-a),
\qquad
B=Z(Z-H(X)).
$$

Define $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$ by

$$
f(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x\in S,\\
1,&x\notin S,
\end{cases}
$$

and assign the constant label $P_L=0$ to every nonvertical affine line and the constant label $P_L=2$ to every vertical affine line. Then $B$ is primitive in $Z$, squarefree, and has weighted degree $D$. Every nonvertical line has exactly $e$ accepted points and satisfies

$$
B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0,
$$

while every vertical line has no accepted points. The test agreement is

$$
\varepsilon=\frac{e}{p+1}=\frac{D-d}{p+1}.
$$
lemmas.title: Strip construction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
On a nonvertical graph with $X$-coordinate $u+vt$, where $v\ne0$,

$$
B(L(t),0)\equiv0,
\qquad
B_Z(L(t),0)=-H(u+vt).
$$

The polynomial $H$ has $e$ distinct roots, and $t\mapsto u+vt$ is a bijective affine map. Hence the pullback has exactly $e$ roots, all simple, and these are precisely the accepted parameters. Since there are $p^2$ nonvertical lines, the ramified-incidence count is $ep^2$, and its normalized measure is

$$
\frac{ep^2}{p^2(p+1)}
=\frac e{p+1}
=\frac{p}{p+1}\frac{D-d}{p}.
$$

At each lifted accepted point,

$$
B_X=B_Y=B_Z=0.
$$

There are $ep$ such lifted points, and each is incident to $p$ accepted nonvertical graph lines, giving $ep^2$ ramified incidences. Counting lifted points rather than incidences therefore does not remove the concurrency loss.

Every supported graph is contained in the factor $C=Z$, for which

$$
\operatorname{wdeg}(C)=d,
\qquad
C_Z=1.
$$

Its factorwise polar loss is therefore $0$. Finally, $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ on the $ep$ points whose first coordinate lies in $S$, so its global agreement is $e/p>e/(p+1)=\varepsilon$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p,d,D,e,S,H,B,f$ and the line labels be as in researcher-0007:P7.1, and put

$$
\tau=\frac{p}{p+1}.
$$

On every nonvertical zero-labelled graph, $B_Z(L(t),0)$ has exactly $D-d$ simple roots, and these roots are exactly the accepted parameters. The whole-relation ramified-incidence measure is

$$
\frac{D-d}{p+1}
=\frac{\tau(D-d)}p
=\varepsilon.
$$

Assigning every supported graph to the factor $C=Z$ gives $C_Z=1$ and factorwise polar loss $0$. The polynomial $Q=0$ has total degree $0$ and global agreement

$$
\frac{D-d}{p}>\varepsilon.
$$
lemmas.title: Polar-loss saturation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
From $p\ge8d$,

$$
\sqrt[3]{dp^2}\ge4d
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sqrt[3]{dp^2}\le\frac p2.
$$

Therefore

$$
e\ge4d,
\qquad
e\le\frac p2+1,
$$

and the stated parameter range gives $2d\le D<p$. Also,

$$
\sqrt[3]{dp^2}\le e\le2\sqrt[3]{dp^2}
$$

and

$$
p\le p+1\le2p.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\frac12\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3}
\le\frac e{p+1}
\le2\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3}.
$$

Since $e\ge4d$, one has $D=d+e=\Theta(e)$. The displayed bounds also give $e=\Theta(\varepsilon p)$, so $D=\Theta(\varepsilon p)$. Finally,

$$
\frac{dp}{\varepsilon}
=\frac{dp(p+1)}e
=\Theta(e^2),
$$

because $e^3=\Theta(dp^2)$. Hence $D=\Theta(\sqrt{dp/\varepsilon})$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $d$ be an integer satisfying

$$
101\le d
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
p\ge8d.
$$

Set

$$
e=\left\lceil(dp^2)^{1/3}\right\rceil,
\qquad
D=d+e,
\qquad
\varepsilon=\frac e{p+1}.
$$

Then

$$
e\ge4d,
\qquad
e\le\frac p2+1,
\qquad
2d\le D<p,
$$

and

$$
\frac12\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3}
\le\varepsilon
\le2\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3}.
$$

For the construction of researcher-0007:P7.1 and researcher-0007:P8.1,

$$
D=\Theta(\varepsilon p)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
D=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\varepsilon}}\right).
$$
lemmas.title: Cubic parameter scale

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The polynomial $Z$ already vanishes on every selected nonvertical graph. Its weighted degree is

$$
\operatorname{wdeg}(Z)=d<D,
$$

and its vertical derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial Z}{\partial Z}=1.
$$

Thus the graph family admits a lower-weight interpolant with no vertical-polar loss. The construction therefore does not force KTZ's minimum-weight interpolant to incur the loss associated with $B$. It refutes only a cleanup claim based on an arbitrary primitive squarefree whole relation and its degree data.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Under the construction of researcher-0007:P7.1 and researcher-0007:P8.1, the interpolant selected by KTZ's minimum-weight rule incurs the whole-relation polar loss

$$
\frac{\tau(D-d)}p.
$$
lemmas.title: Minimum-interpolant saturation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
In characteristic $p$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial Z}(Z^p-X)=pZ^{p-1}=0.
$$

The polynomial is primitive in $Z$ and squarefree, but its weighted degree is

$$
\operatorname{wdeg}(Z^p-X)=pd.
$$

Since $d\ge101$, this does not satisfy the required inequality $\delta<p$. The example is excluded from the campaign regime and does not refute the factorwise theorem.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with $X,Y,Z$ carrying weights $1,1,d$. Under the campaign requirement that a relation have weighted degree $\delta<p$, the polynomial

$$
B=Z^p-X
$$

is an inseparability counterexample to the factorwise theorem.
lemmas.title: Inseparability attempt

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If correct labels are concentrated in exactly $k$ direction classes and $f=0$, the exact local agreement is

$$
\varepsilon=\frac{k}{p+1}.
$$

The polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ at every point. Moreover, the carrying factor $C=Z$ satisfies $C_Z=1$. Thus the instance has a perfect global decoder and no factorwise polar obstruction. It refutes neither the factorwise theorem nor the soundness benchmark.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $1\le k\le p+1$. An instance with $f=0$ whose correct labels are concentrated in exactly $k$ direction classes refutes the factorwise theorem in the campaign regime.
lemmas.title: Direction-concentration attempt

dependencies: Hall's marriage theorem, proved in the step by regular degree counting
lemmas.proof_markdown:
For each $b\in\mathbb F_p$, add a dummy point vertex $z_b$. Join $z_b$ to the $p$ finite-slope lines $y=mx+b$, with $m\in\mathbb F_p$, and to the vertical line $x=b$. The augmented graph has $p^2+p=p(p+1)$ point-side vertices and $p(p+1)$ line-side vertices. Every real or dummy point has degree $p+1$, and every affine line has its $p$ real points and one dummy neighbor, so the augmented graph is balanced and $(p+1)$-regular.

For any left-side vertex set $S$, its $(p+1)\lvert S\rvert$ edges enter $N(S)$, whose vertices have at most $(p+1)\lvert N(S)\rvert$ incident slots. Hence

$$(p+1)\lvert S\rvert\le (p+1)\lvert N(S)\rvert,$$

so Hall's condition holds and the augmented graph has a perfect matching. Removing that matching preserves balanced regularity. Iteration decomposes the augmented graph into $p+1$ perfect matchings, which are taken as colors.

After the dummy edges are deleted, every real point retains exactly one edge of every color. Every affine line loses exactly the color of its unique dummy edge. Each perfect matching contains one edge at each of the $p$ dummy vertices, with distinct line endpoints, so each color is absent from exactly $p$ affine lines.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, let $\mathcal P=\mathbb F_p^2$, let $\mathcal L$ be the set of affine lines in $\mathbb F_p^2$, and let

$$E=\{(x,L)\in\mathcal P\times\mathcal L:x\in L\}.$$

There is a partition of $E$ into $p+1$ color classes such that every point is incident to exactly one edge of each color, every affine line is incident to exactly one edge of all but one color and to no edge of the remaining color, and every color is omitted by exactly $p$ affine lines.
lemmas.title: Affine incidence decomposition

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Select $d$ colors and let $E_0$ consist of their real incidence edges. Every point has $E_0$-degree $d$. A line has degree $d$ unless its unique missing color was selected, in which case it has degree $d-1$. Each selected color is absent from exactly $p$ lines, and each line misses only one color, so there are exactly $pd$ distinct deficient lines.

Put

$$r=p+1-d>0.$$

Form the bipartite repair graph whose left vertices are the deficient lines and whose edges are their unselected real incidences. Every deficient line misses a selected color and therefore has all $r$ unselected colors, so every left degree is $r$. Every point has one edge of each unselected color before restriction, so every right degree is at most $r$. For every deficient-line set $S$,

$$r\lvert S\rvert=e(S,N(S))\le r\lvert N(S)\rvert.$$

Hall's theorem therefore supplies a matching saturating all deficient lines. Adding its edges to $E_0$ raises each deficient line from degree $d-1$ to degree $d$ and leaves every other line at degree $d$. The matching has $pd$ distinct point endpoints, which acquire degree $d+1$; the remaining $p^2-pd=p(p-d)$ points retain degree $d$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. The affine point-line incidence graph over $\mathbb F_p^2$ has a spanning subgraph in which every affine line has degree $d$, exactly $pd$ points have degree $d+1$, and the remaining $p(p-d)$ points have degree $d$.
lemmas.title: Regular incidence carrier

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $f=0$. For each affine line $L$, let

$$S_L=\{t\in\mathbb F_p:(L(t),L)\in E(H)\}.$$

Every line has degree $d$ in $H$, so $\lvert S_L\rvert=d$. Define

$$P_L(t)=\prod_{a\in S_L}(t-a).$$

The parameters in $S_L$ are distinct. Since $d<p$, the product has formal degree exactly $d$ and vanishes in $\mathbb F_p$ exactly on $S_L$, with no polynomial-function aliasing. Thus $P_L(t)=f(L(t))$ holds exactly at the incidences of $H$. Fixed affine parameterizations include vertical lines and require no slope division.

There are $p(p+1)$ affine lines, each with $d$ accepted points. Hence the table has $p(p+1)d$ accepted incidences among $p^2(p+1)$ total incidences, and

$$\epsilon=\frac{p(p+1)d}{p^2(p+1)}=\frac dp.$$

Every line supports acceptance. Finally, the total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ is legal under the ambient degree cap and agrees with $f$ at every point.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $H$ be the spanning incidence subgraph supplied by P2. For every affine line $L$, fix an affine bijection $t\mapsto L(t)$ from $\mathbb F_p$ onto $L$. There exist a point table $f\colon\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$ and labels $P_L\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ with $\deg P_L=d$ such that

$$P_L(t)=f(L(t))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (L(t),L)\in E(H).$$

The resulting table has agreement $\epsilon=d/p$, every affine line has exactly $d$ accepted points, every point has accepted degree $d$ or $d+1$, exactly $pd$ points have accepted degree $d+1$, every affine line supports acceptance, and the total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ everywhere.
lemmas.title: Polynomial carrier realization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Define the larger self-inclusive capped load

$$v_x=\min\left\{1,\sum_{\substack{M\in\mathcal L\\x\in M}}A(x,M)\lambda_M\right\}.$$

For every accepted incidence $(x,L)$, one has $u_{x,L}(\lambda)\le v_x$. Since every line has $d$ accepted points, there are $p(p+1)$ lines, and $a_x\le d+1$, double counting gives

$$\theta d\,p(p+1)\le\sum_{L\in\mathcal L}\sum_{x\in N_E(L)}u_{x,L}(\lambda)\le\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^2}a_xv_x\le(d+1)\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^2}v_x.$$

Nonnegativity of the weights gives

$$\sum_xv_x\le\sum_x\sum_{\substack{M\in\mathcal L\\x\in M}}A(x,M)\lambda_M=\sum_{M\in\mathcal L}\lvert N_E(M)\rvert\lambda_M=d\sum_{M\in\mathcal L}\lambda_M.$$

Combining the two displays and dividing by $d>0$ yields the claimed lower bound. No Markov inequality, union bound, or Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used. Indicator weights are ordinary selected-line families, so the same bound applies to that special case and to the stricter other-line reaching condition.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For the table constructed in P3, write $\mathcal L$ for the affine lines, $A(x,L)\in\{0,1\}$ for the acceptance indicator,

$$N_E(L)=\{x\in L:A(x,L)=1\},\qquad a_x=\sum_{L\ni x}A(x,L).$$

Let $0<\theta\le1$, let $\lambda=(\lambda_M)_{M\in\mathcal L}$ be nonnegative line weights, and define

$$u_{x,L}(\lambda)=\min\left\{1,\sum_{\substack{M\ni x\\M\ne L}}A(x,M)\lambda_M\right\}$$

for every accepted incidence $(x,L)$. If

$$\sum_{x\in N_E(L)}u_{x,L}(\lambda)\ge\theta\lvert N_E(L)\rvert$$

for every $L\in\mathcal L$, then

$$\sum_{M\in\mathcal L}\lambda_M\ge\frac{\theta p(p+1)}{d+1}.$$

The same conclusion holds when every $\lambda_M$ belongs to $\{0,1\}$.
lemmas.title: Fractional reaching lower bound

lemmas.proof_markdown:
At every accepted incidence $(x,L)$, the number of other accepted lines through $x$ is

$$a_x-1\ge d-1.$$

For the uniform weights,

$$\sum_{\substack{M\ni x\\M\ne L}}A(x,M)\lambda_M\ge(d-1)\frac{\theta}{d-1}=\theta.$$

Because $\theta\le1$, capping the load at $1$ still gives $u_{x,L}(\lambda)\ge\theta$. Hence the weights are $\theta$-reaching. Since $\lvert\mathcal L\rvert=p(p+1)$, their total weight is

$$\sum_{M\in\mathcal L}\lambda_M=p(p+1)\frac{\theta}{d-1}.$$

The ratio of this value to the lower-bound value $\theta p(p+1)/(d+1)$ is $(d+1)/(d-1)$. Since $d\ge101$,

$$\frac{d+1}{d-1}\le\frac{102}{100}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For the table constructed in P3 and every $0<\theta\le1$, assign every affine line the weight

$$\lambda_M=\frac{\theta}{d-1}.$$

These weights are $\theta$-reaching through other accepted lines and have total weight

$$\frac{\theta p(p+1)}{d-1}.$$

If $\operatorname{OPT}_\theta$ is the infimum of the total weight over all nonnegative $\theta$-reaching weights, then

$$\operatorname{OPT}_\theta\le\frac{\theta p(p+1)}{d-1},$$

and the multiplicative gap between this upper bound and the lower-bound value $\theta p(p+1)/(d+1)$ is

$$\frac{d+1}{d-1}\le\frac{102}{100}.$$
lemmas.title: Uniform reaching weights

lemmas.proof_markdown:
At a fixed point $x$, exactly $a_x(a_x-1)$ ordered pairs of distinct incident lines are jointly accepted. Since there are $p(p+1)$ ordered pairs of distinct lines through $x$,

$$\Gamma_2=\frac{\mathbb E_x[a_x(a_x-1)]}{p(p+1)}.$$

The mean accepted degree is

$$\mathbb E_x[a_x]=(p+1)\epsilon.$$

Using $\mathbb E_x[a_x^2]=(\mathbb E_x[a_x])^2+\operatorname{Var}_x(a_x)$ gives

$$\Gamma_2=\frac{(p+1)^2\epsilon^2-(p+1)\epsilon+\operatorname{Var}_x(a_x)}{p(p+1)},$$

which simplifies to the asserted identity. Nonnegativity of the variance gives

$$\Gamma_2\ge\epsilon^2-\frac{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}p.$$

If $\epsilon\ge2/p$, then $\epsilon(1-\epsilon)/p\le\epsilon/p\le\epsilon^2/2$, and therefore $\Gamma_2\ge\epsilon^2/2$. This is the exact variance, or Jensen, loss; no further concentration loss occurs.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and consider any valid affine line-versus-point table over $\mathbb F_p^2$ with line-label degree at most $d$. Let $A(x,L)$ be its acceptance indicator, let

$$\epsilon=\frac{\sum_{x,L\ni x}A(x,L)}{p^2(p+1)},\qquad a_x=\sum_{L\ni x}A(x,L),$$

and let $\Gamma_2$ be the probability that a uniformly chosen ordered pair of distinct lines through a uniformly chosen point are both accepted there. Then

$$\Gamma_2=\epsilon^2-\frac{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}p+\frac{\operatorname{Var}_x(a_x)}{p(p+1)}.$$
lemmas.title: Two-line collision identity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose $k$ projective direction classes. Set $f=0$, label every affine line in a chosen direction by the zero polynomial, and label every other affine line by the constant-one polynomial. Every point lies on exactly one affine line in each projective direction, so precisely $k$ lines through each point accept. Thus $a_x=k$ identically and $\operatorname{Var}_x(a_x)=0$.

The agreement and ordered collision probability are

$$\epsilon=\frac{k}{p+1},\qquad \Gamma_2=\frac{k(k-1)}{p(p+1)}.$$

Substitution into P6 gives equality in its lower bound. The constant labels have formal degree $0$ and are legal under the ambient degree-at-most-$d$ rule; the ambient test cap remains $d>100$. Finally, $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ everywhere, so its global agreement is $1$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $1\le k\le p+1$ be an integer. There is a valid affine line-versus-point table over $\mathbb F_p^2$ with degree-at-most-$d$ labels such that every point has accepted degree $k$,

$$\epsilon=\frac{k}{p+1},\qquad \operatorname{Var}_x(a_x)=0,
\qquad \Gamma_2=\frac{k(k-1)}{p(p+1)}.$$

The collision lower bound in P6 is attained, and the total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ has global agreement $1$.
lemmas.title: Direction-class equality

lemmas.proof_markdown:
KTZ Lemma 3.2 samples at rate $\Theta(1/(\epsilon p))$. Its Chernoff estimate and union bound over at most $p(p+1)$ target lines, together with Chebyshev's inequality for the sample size, cost only constants and yield only the one-sided bound

$$\lvert R\rvert=O\left(\frac p\epsilon\right).$$

Weighted interpolation then gives

$$D=O\left(\sqrt{d\lvert R\rvert}\right)=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}\right).$$

The distinct-root and lifting budgets require $D=O(\epsilon p)$. Squaring the resulting scale comparison gives

$$\frac{dp}{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^2p^2),$$

or equivalently $\epsilon^3=\Omega(d/p)$. KTZ does not assert simultaneous $\Theta$-saturation of these estimates.

The regular-carrier construction separately rules out a universal fractional cover of weight $o(p/\epsilon)$. Its perfect decoder $Q=0$ may nevertheless be found before interpolation, so the construction does not make the cubic gate necessary for every decoding architecture.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $\epsilon>0$. Suppose a reaching family $R$ and a weighted interpolation degree $D$ satisfy

$$\lvert R\rvert=O\left(\frac p\epsilon\right),\qquad D=O\left(\sqrt{d\lvert R\rvert}\right)=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}\right),$$

and suppose the distinct-root and lifting budget imposes $D=O(\epsilon p)$. Then the resulting parameter threshold is

$$\epsilon^3=\Omega\left(\frac dp\right).$$
lemmas.title: KTZ exponent reconstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
KTZ Lemma 2.1 gives the absolute affine form of Vinh's spectral estimate with normalized error $(p+1)^{-1/2}$. KTZ Lemma 6.2 absorbs that error only under

$$(p+1)^{-1/2}\le\frac{\epsilon}{8000}.$$

At the cubic threshold the condition is weaker, since

$$\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3}\sqrt p=d^{1/3}p^{1/6}.$$

For the parameters in the statement,

$$\epsilon\sqrt p=C\,101^\alpha p^{1/2-\alpha}\longrightarrow0.$$

Thus the absorption inequality fails for all sufficiently large $p$. This is an obstruction to the Vinh-only recovery method, not a counterexample to a stronger soundness theorem.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $C>0$ and $\alpha>1/2$, set $d=101$, and let $p>101$ tend to infinity through primes. If

$$\epsilon=C\left(\frac{101}{p}\right)^\alpha,$$

then $\epsilon\sqrt p\to0$, and the absorption condition

$$(p+1)^{-1/2}\le\frac{\epsilon}{8000}$$

fails for all sufficiently large $p$. The KTZ/Vinh component-recovery step does not yield its linear global-agreement conclusion in this regime.
lemmas.title: Vinh recovery barrier

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Minimum degree gives $kN\le I(P,T)$. Theorem 3 gives

$$kN\ll N^{22/15},$$

and hence $N\gg k^{15/7}$. For this lower-bound scale to be at least $kp$, one needs

$$k^{15/7}\gtrsim kp,$$

which is equivalent to $k^{8/7}\gtrsim p$ and therefore requires $k\gtrsim p^{7/8}$. At that scale, $N\gtrsim p^{15/8}$.

The characteristic hypothesis specializes to

$$N^{-2}N^{13}=N^{11}\ll p^{15},$$

or $N\ll p^{15/11}$. Hence there is no asymptotic overlap. This calculation concerns distinct unweighted lines and is an exponent reconstruction from the quoted theorem, not a low-degree-test conclusion stated by Stevens–de Zeeuw.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, let $P\subseteq\mathbb F_p^2$ contain $N$ points, and let $T$ be a set of $N$ distinct affine lines. Suppose their incidence graph has minimum degree at least $k$ and satisfies the hypotheses of Stevens–de Zeeuw Theorem 3,

$$\lvert P\rvert^{7/8}<\lvert T\rvert<\lvert P\rvert^{8/7},\qquad \lvert P\rvert^{-2}\lvert T\rvert^{13}\ll p^{15}.$$

Then

$$N\gg k^{15/7}.$$

For this lower-bound scale to reach $N=\Omega(kp)$, one must have $k\gtrsim p^{7/8}$ and $N\gtrsim p^{15/8}$, which is outside the characteristic range $N\ll p^{15/11}$.
lemmas.title: Balanced incidence diagnostic

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Minimum degree gives $kN\le I(P,T)$. In the balanced Cartesian case, Theorem 4 gives

$$kN\ll N^{11/8}+N.$$

Once the linear term is absorbed, this yields $N\gg k^{8/3}$. For this scale to be at least $kp$, one needs

$$k^{8/3}\gtrsim kp,$$

so $k^{5/3}\gtrsim p$ and $k\gtrsim p^{3/5}$. It then forces $N\gtrsim p^{8/5}$.

The positive-characteristic condition becomes

$$\lvert A\rvert\lvert T\rvert=N^{1/2}N=N^{3/2}\ll p^2,$$

or $N\ll p^{4/3}$. Hence there is again no asymptotic overlap. The calculation requires a genuine Cartesian point set and distinct unweighted lines; it is an exponent reconstruction from the quoted theorem, not a source-stated low-degree-test conclusion.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, let $P=A\times B\subseteq\mathbb F_p^2$ satisfy $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert=\sqrt N$, and let $T$ be a set of $N$ distinct affine lines. Suppose the incidence graph has minimum degree at least $k$, the linear term in the incidence estimate is absorbed, and the hypotheses of Stevens–de Zeeuw Theorem 4 hold:

$$\lvert A\rvert\le\lvert B\rvert,
\qquad \lvert A\rvert\lvert B\rvert^2\le\lvert T\rvert^3,
\qquad \lvert A\rvert\lvert T\rvert\ll p^2.$$

Then

$$N\gg k^{8/3}.$$

For this lower-bound scale to reach $N=\Omega(kp)$, one must have $k\gtrsim p^{3/5}$ and $N\gtrsim p^{8/5}$, which is outside the characteristic range $N\ll p^{4/3}$.
lemmas.title: Cartesian incidence diagnostic

lemmas.proof_markdown: P6 and P7 show that the concentrated-direction table attains the quadratic collision lower bound, so acceptance density alone does not force compatible-pair density $\omega(\epsilon^2)$. P4 and P5 show that the regular carrier requires fractional reaching weight of order $p/\epsilon$ for any fixed positive reaching fraction, so acceptance density alone does not force an $o(p/\epsilon)$ universal reaching family. Both constructions have $f=0$ and the perfect decoder $Q=0$. They therefore refute only the incidence-only shortcut, not soundness.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For every valid affine line-versus-point table of acceptance density $\epsilon$, acceptance density alone yields either compatible distinct-line-pair density $\omega(\epsilon^2)$ or a nonnegative line-weight family of total weight $o(p/\epsilon)$ that reaches a fixed positive fraction of the accepted points of every accepted line through other accepted lines.
lemmas.title: Incidence-only shortcut

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The table has $p^2(p+1)\epsilon$ accepted incidences. Double counting them by their point and line endpoints gives
